subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
passage: I am Shalini and I sit next to Arohi in art class. Last Monday she told me she was starting to draw for real. I expected a huge plan, but she said, "Ten minutes a day, that is all. My cousin planned two hours daily and stopped by Thursday. A tiny habit that carries on beats a big one that dies." Every afternoon after that I saw her at the window seat with her sketchbook and a timer on the sill, drawing pots and shoes until it beeped. She stopped even when she was halfway through a leaf. By the third week her sketchbook was fat. I cannot tell if she ever wanted to do more; she just kept going.

qa.q: How many minutes a day did Arohi decide to draw?
qa.a: Arohi decided to draw for ten minutes a day.

qa.q: What was Arohi worried about when she chose such a small amount?
qa.a: That a big plan would fail after a few days, as her cousin's did, so she wanted a habit that would carry on.

qa.q: What could Arohi do when ten minutes starts to feel easy?
qa.a: Add a few minutes slowly or set a small goal, such as one finished drawing a week, because growth stays steady that way.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Arohi stopping halfway through a leaf?
qa.a: With some puzzlement and admiration for the discipline, though Shalini admits she cannot tell whether Arohi wanted to do more.

grounding: A girl beginning drawing chooses ten minutes a day, judging a small habit that continues better than a big plan that stops.
